en: Difficult to understand; obscure
hook: ABSTRUSE: ABSTRACT and CONFUSE.
story: Abstruse. On the first day of a quantum mechanics course, a visiting professor filled four whiteboards with symbols, spoke of Hilbert spaces and eigenstates, and never once gave an example. By the end, even the top students were staring blankly. Kamal whispered to Rafi, "The only word I understood was hello." The lecture was abstruse: difficult to understand, obscure. In Latin, abstrusus means hidden away. Do not confuse it with obtuse, meaning slow witted. Synonyms: recondite, esoteric, arcane.

gre.s: Although the philosopher's early essays were lucid and accessible, his later work grew so ____ that even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments.
gre.clue: even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments

en: Providing additional help or support
hook: AUXILIARY: AUX cable, extra support.
story: Auxiliary. During a power cut at a Dhaka hospital, the lights in the operating theatre flickered off for two seconds, then came back on as the auxiliary generator started humming. The surgeons never even paused. An auxiliary generator provides additional help or support when the main system fails. In grammar, auxiliary verbs like have and will help the main verb. The word comes from the Latin auxilium, meaning help. Synonyms: supplementary, backup, ancillary.

gre.s: Although the main pump handles routine cooling, engineers installed ____ pumps that switch on automatically whenever demand exceeds its capacity.
gre.clue: whenever demand exceeds its capacity

en: A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect
hook: CARICATURE: a CARtoon that exaggerates.
story: Caricature. At the Ekushey book fair, a street artist drew Arif in two minutes for fifty taka. The drawing gave him an enormous head, a huge toothy grin, and glasses the size of dinner plates, yet everyone recognised him instantly. It was a caricature: a picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect. Political cartoonists draw caricatures of leaders. The word comes from the Italian caricare, to load or overload. Synonyms: parody, lampoon, burlesque.

gre.s: The novel's portrait of the professor is less a realistic character study than a ____: his vanity is so inflated and his absent-mindedness so extreme that no reader could mistake him for a real person.
gre.clue: no reader could mistake him for a real person

en: Moral corruption; wickedness
hook: DEPRAVITY: DEPRIVED of all goodness.
story: Depravity. The detective novel Shuvo was reading described a villain who poisoned his own brother for an inheritance, then framed a loyal servant and smiled as the innocent man was led away. Shuvo put the book down, disturbed by such depravity: moral corruption, wickedness. Depraved comes from the Latin pravus, meaning crooked; a depraved person is morally twisted. Do not confuse it with deprivation, which means lacking necessities. Synonyms: wickedness, corruption, vice, degeneracy.

gre.s: The prosecutor described the crimes as acts of shocking ____, committed not out of desperation but out of sheer delight in the suffering of others.
gre.clue: sheer delight in the suffering of others

en: A person with a superficial interest in an art or field
hook: DILETTANTE: DELIGHTS in dabbling, but never goes deep.
story: Dilettante. In January, Farhan bought a guitar. In February, he switched to painting. By April he was learning Japanese, and by June he had decided to become a photographer. He never got past the basics of anything, and the guitar now gathers dust. His friends tease him as a dilettante: a person with only a superficial interest in an art or field. It comes from the Italian dilettare, to delight; a dilettante dabbles for pleasure rather than mastery. Synonyms: dabbler, amateur.

gre.s: Though he described himself as a serious scholar of Persian poetry, he was really a ____, having skimmed a few translations without ever studying the language.
gre.clue: having skimmed a few translations without ever studying the language

en: Shameless boldness; insolent nerve
hook: EFFRONTERY: right in your FRONT, shamelessly.
story: Effrontery. A student was caught copying answers from his phone during an exam. When the invigilator confiscated the phone, the student demanded it back and insisted that the invigilator apologise for disturbing his concentration. The whole hall gasped at his effrontery: shameless boldness, insolent nerve. The word comes from the Latin effrons, barefaced, from frons, the forehead: someone with a brazen face who cannot blush. Compare temerity, which is rash boldness. Synonyms: impudence, gall, audacity.

gre.s: Caught plagiarizing an entire chapter, the author had the ____ to accuse his critics of jealousy, as though they rather than he were at fault.
gre.clue: as though they rather than he were at fault

en: To gradually intrude beyond proper limits
hook: EN-CROACH: like a COCKROACH creeping into your space.
story: Encroach. Each year, a factory beside a river near Dhaka moved its boundary wall a few meters closer to the water, filling the bank with sand and building new sheds. Environmental groups complained that it was encroaching on public land: gradually intruding beyond proper limits. Encroachment on rivers and footpaths is a constant problem in the city. The word comes from old French for catching with a hook, as if snatching land bit by bit. Synonyms: intrude, trespass, impinge.

gre.s: Residents worried that the expanding city would gradually ____ on the surrounding farmland, swallowing a few more fields each year until none remained.
gre.clue: swallowing a few more fields each year

en: To give a quality or ability; to provide a permanent income
hook: ENDOW: give a DOWRY of talent or money.
story: Endow. When a retired jute merchant died, his will left a large sum to his old school in Comilla. The money was invested, and its yearly income now pays for twenty scholarships, year after year, forever. He had endowed the school: provided it with a permanent income. Endow also means to give a quality or ability, as in nature endowed her with a beautiful voice. A university's endowment is its permanent fund. Synonyms: fund, bestow, furnish, imbue.

gre.s: Critics complained that the novelist tended to ____ his villains with such charm and wit that readers found them far more appealing than his heroes.
gre.clue: readers found them far more appealing than his heroes

en: To ask someone earnestly or anxiously
hook: EN-TREAT: begging for a TREAT.
story: Entreat. When Tanvir won a scholarship to study in Germany, his mother wept and entreated him to stay. "Please, my son, we will find you a good job here. Do not go so far away." She held his hands and asked him again and again. To entreat is to ask someone earnestly or anxiously, almost to beg. An entreaty is an earnest plea. Do not confuse it with entice, which means to tempt. Synonyms: implore, beseech, plead.

gre.s: Knowing that the king rarely granted pardons, the condemned man's family chose not to demand mercy but to ____ him for it, kneeling humbly before the throne.
gre.clue: kneeling humbly before the throne

en: Fond of company; sociable
hook: GREGARIOUS: GREG is in every group (grex = herd).
story: Gregarious. On her first day at the hostel, Sara knew no one. By dinner, she had learned the name of everyone on her floor, organised a tea party in the common room, and joined three clubs. Her roommate, who preferred books to people, watched in amazement. Sara was gregarious: fond of company, sociable. It comes from the Latin grex, flock, as in congregation; gregarious animals like sheep live in herds. Its opposite is reclusive. Synonyms: sociable, outgoing, convivial.

gre.s: Unlike his ____ brother, who thrived at crowded parties and made friends wherever he went, the poet preferred long solitary walks and the company of books.
gre.clue: thrived at crowded parties and made friends wherever he went

en: A formal charge of a serious crime; a strong criticism
hook: INDICTMENT (in-DITE-ment): the court DICTATES charges.
story: Indictment. After months of investigation, prosecutors announced an indictment of a bank director, formally charging him with embezzling millions. The next morning, a newspaper editorial called the scandal an indictment of the entire banking system: a strong criticism showing how badly it had failed. Note the pronunciation: the c is silent, so it sounds like in dite ment. To indict is to charge formally with a crime. Synonyms: charge, accusation; and for the second sense, condemnation, censure.

gre.s: The report was a damning ____ of the agency's leadership, detailing years of ignored warnings, falsified data, and entirely preventable deaths.
gre.clue: detailing years of ignored warnings

en: Angry at something unjust
hook: INDIGNANT: your DIGNITY was insulted.
story: Indignant. At a government office, Rahim waited four hours in line to renew his passport. Then a man in a suit walked straight to the counter, slipped the clerk an envelope, and was served at once. Rahim was indignant: angry at something unjust. He stood up and demanded to know why bribes came before citizens. Indignant comes from the Latin for unworthy; we feel indignant when something unworthy is done. Indignation is righteous anger. Synonyms: outraged, aggrieved, incensed.

gre.s: Accused of a theft she had not committed, the housekeeper was not frightened but ____, demanding an apology from the family that had wrongly suspected her.
gre.clue: a theft she had not committed

en: Unable to be avoided; inevitable
hook: IN-E-LUCTABLE: you can't struggle (luctari) out of it.
story: Ineluctable. Imran tried everything to avoid the final calculus exam. He hoped for a strike, a flood, even a cyclone. None came. The exam date arrived, as exam dates always do. Some things are ineluctable: impossible to avoid; inevitable. Ageing, death, and deadlines are ineluctable. The word comes from the Latin luctari, to wrestle or struggle; something ineluctable is a thing you cannot wrestle your way out of. Synonyms: inevitable, inescapable, unavoidable.

gre.s: Many historians once believed the empire's decline was ____, the result of forces no ruler could have resisted; newer scholarship stresses specific mistakes that might easily have been avoided.
gre.clue: forces no ruler could have resisted

en: Curious; eager for knowledge
hook: INQUISITIVE: always INQUIRING.
story: Inquisitive. Mitu's little nephew asked forty questions in a single afternoon. Why is the sky blue? Where do clouds go at night? Why do fish not drown? How does the phone know my voice? He opened every drawer and took apart a broken radio to see what was inside. He was inquisitive: curious and eager for knowledge. Inquisitive shares a root with inquiry and question. It can also suggest being nosy about other people's affairs. Synonyms: curious, inquiring, probing.

gre.s: Endlessly ____, the young scientist pestered her mentors with questions and spent her weekends dismantling old instruments to learn how they worked.
gre.clue: pestered her mentors with questions

en: Freedom from restrictions; scope for action
hook: LATITUDE: lots of room, wide like LATITUDE lines across the globe.
story: Latitude. Most of Nadia's friends had office jobs with strict hours and fixed tasks. At her new tech startup, the manager told her, "Work when you like, from where you like, and choose your own projects, as long as the product improves." Nadia loved the latitude: freedom from restrictions, scope for action. In geography, latitude measures distance north or south of the equator, along lines that stretch wide around the globe. Latin latus means wide. Synonyms: freedom, leeway, scope.

gre.s: The new editor gave her reporters considerable ____, allowing them to pursue whatever stories interested them rather than assigning topics herself.
gre.clue: rather than assigning topics herself

en: Treating serious matters with humor or lack of respect
hook: LEVITY: LIGHT as LEVITATING.
story: Levity. At a serious faculty meeting about falling exam results, a young lecturer joked that perhaps the students were studying the wrong syllabus on purpose. A few people laughed, but the dean frowned. This was no time for levity: treating serious matters with humor or a lack of respect. Levity comes from the Latin levis, light, as in levitate; it is lightness where weight is expected. Its opposite is gravity, meaning seriousness. Synonyms: frivolity, flippancy, jocularity.

gre.s: The speaker's ____ seemed badly misjudged; his jokes about the earthquake offended an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims.
gre.clue: an audience that had gathered to mourn its victims

en: Wishing to do evil to others
hook: MALE-VOLENT: wishing (vol) BAD (mal).
story: Malevolent. In the folk tales Tania's grandmother told on winter nights, a malevolent spirit lived in the old banyan tree. It wished harm on every traveler, leading them into swamps at night and whispering lies to turn brothers against each other. Malevolent means wishing to do evil to others. Mal means bad, and volent means wishing, as in volunteer. Its opposite is benevolent, wishing good. Synonyms: malicious, spiteful, malign, hostile.

gre.s: Far from being a neutral observer, the narrator is quietly ____, manipulating the other characters purely for the pleasure of watching them suffer.
gre.clue: purely for the pleasure of watching them suffer

en: To intervene to help resolve a dispute
hook: MEDIATE: stand in the MIDDLE.
story: Mediate. Two families in a village near Bogura had argued for years over the boundary between their fields. Fights broke out at every harvest. Finally the old schoolteacher, respected by both sides, agreed to mediate. He listened to each family, walked the land with them, and proposed a fair line that both accepted. To mediate is to intervene between parties to help resolve a dispute. A mediator stands in the middle, from the Latin medius. Synonyms: arbitrate, intercede, broker.

gre.s: Because neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly, both agreed to let a neutral diplomat ____ the dispute over the contested border.
gre.clue: neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly

en: To block or obstruct
hook: OCCLUDE: CLOSE it off (claudere = to close).
story: Occlude. Zayan's grandfather had chest pain, and the doctor showed the family an image of his heart. Fatty plaque had built up in one artery until it almost completely blocked the flow of blood. "This artery is occluded," she said. To occlude is to block or obstruct. During a solar eclipse, the moon occludes the sun. The clude part comes from the Latin claudere, to close, as in exclude and include: think of closing something off. Synonyms: block, obstruct, clog.

gre.s: The tall new apartment towers threaten to ____ the river view from the old houses, which until now have looked directly onto the water.
gre.clue: which until now have looked directly onto the water

en: To calm someone's anger or agitation
hook: PACIFY: make PEACE (pax), like a baby's PACIFIER.
story: Pacify. A toddler on the crowded bus to Cox's Bazar began to scream. Passengers glared. His mother tried a biscuit, a song, and a toy, and finally lifted him to the window, where he saw the sea for the first time and fell silent. She had pacified him: calmed his anger and agitation. Pacify shares a root with peace and with the Pacific, the peaceful ocean. A baby's dummy is called a pacifier. Synonyms: placate, soothe, appease, mollify.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced the chief executive's resignation and promised a full independent investigation.
gre.clue: the furious shareholders

en: A model of excellence; a perfect example
hook: PARAGON: PARAmount, the top example.
story: Paragon. In Anika's family, every child was compared to cousin Mahin: top marks, polite to elders, generous to the poor, captain of the cricket team, and he even helped his mother cook. Anika rolled her eyes. "Yes, yes, Mahin is a paragon," she sighed: a model of excellence, a perfect example. Paragon comes from an old Italian word for a touchstone used to test gold. A paragon of virtue is the standard others are measured by. Synonyms: model, exemplar, epitome.

gre.s: Admired throughout her long career as a ____ of integrity, the judge stunned the public when evidence emerged that she had accepted bribes for years.
gre.clue: Admired throughout her long career

en: To treat with apparent kindness that reveals a feeling of superiority; also, to be a customer of
bn: অনুগ্রহ দেখানোর ভান করা; নিয়মিত খরিদ্দার হওয়া
hook: PATRONIZE: acting like a 'PATRON' to someone below you.
story: Patronize. When Priya joined an engineering firm, an older colleague explained the computer's power button to her very slowly, then praised her for being brave enough to study engineering as a girl. Priya had a master's degree in robotics. He was patronizing her: treating her with apparent kindness that revealed a feeling of superiority. Patronize also means to be a regular customer: Priya patronizes the tea stall outside the office. Synonyms for the first sense: condescend, talk down to.

gre.s: Although the minister meant to sound sympathetic, his habit of explaining simple ideas to the farmers slowly and loudly seemed to ____ them, and they left the meeting insulted.
gre.clue: they left the meeting insulted

en: Extremely poor; also, extremely stingy
hook: PENURIOUS: without a PENNY.
story: Penurious. Rumana's landlord owns six buildings in Dhanmondi, yet he wears the same torn sandals every day, refuses to fix a leaking tap, and argues with the vegetable seller over two taka. Rich in property, he is penurious in spirit: extremely stingy. The word can also mean extremely poor, since penury means poverty. Both senses come from the Latin penuria, want or need. Context tells you which: a penurious miser, or a penurious student. Synonyms: miserly, parsimonious; or impoverished.

gre.s: Despite his considerable fortune, the old collector was so ____ that he refused to heat his house in winter and haggled fiercely over the price of bread.
gre.clue: refused to heat his house in winter

en: Having a pleasantly sharp, spicy taste; stimulating and interesting
hook: PIQUANT (PEE-kunt): it PIQUES your tastebuds.
story: Piquant. Lamia's grandmother makes a famous fish curry with green chilies, mustard, and a squeeze of lime. The first bite is sharp and spicy, then tangy and fresh, and everyone asks for more. Her curry is piquant: having a pleasantly sharp, spicy taste. Piquant can also describe something stimulating and interesting, like a piquant bit of gossip. It comes from the French piquer, to prick or sting. Synonyms: tangy, zesty, spicy; or intriguing, provocative.

gre.s: Though the biography covers familiar territory, its ____ anecdotes about the poet's feuds and love affairs keep readers engaged from beginning to end.
gre.clue: keep readers engaged from beginning to end

en: Spreading unchecked; widespread and uncontrolled
hook: RAMPANT: RAMPAGING everywhere.
story: Rampant. During one monsoon, dengue spread through a Dhaka neighborhood from house to house, then street to street, faster than the hospitals could treat patients. Health officials described the disease as rampant: spreading unchecked, widespread and uncontrolled. Corruption, inflation, and rumours can also be rampant. Originally, rampant described a lion on a coat of arms, rearing up on its hind legs, wild and threatening. Synonyms: unchecked, rife, widespread, unbridled.

gre.s: In the absence of any regulatory oversight, fraud became ____ in the industry, spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete.
gre.clue: spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete

en: Far away; distant; slight or faint
hook: REMOTE: far away like a REMOTE village, or a remote chance.
story: Remote. Sabbir's grandparents live in a remote char village in the middle of the Jamuna, far from any town and reachable only by boat. But on the GRE, remote often has another sense: slight or faint. When Sabbir asked whether the ferry would run during the storm, the boatman laughed. "There is only a remote possibility." Remote can also describe a person who is distant and aloof. Synonyms: distant, isolated; or slight, faint, slim.

gre.s: Although the doctors admitted there was a ____ chance that the experimental treatment would succeed, they warned the family not to raise their hopes.
gre.clue: warned the family not to raise their hopes

en: An unprincipled person
hook: REPROBATE: REPROVED and BEATEN by society.
story: Reprobate. Everyone in the neighborhood knew Babu's uncle. He gambled away his wife's jewelry, borrowed money from every relative without repaying a taka, lied to the police, and laughed about it all at the tea stall. The elders called him a reprobate: an unprincipled person, beyond moral correction. The word comes from the Latin for disapproved or rejected; in old religious language, a reprobate was someone damned. Synonyms: scoundrel, rogue, miscreant, degenerate.

gre.s: Though the novel's hero is a charming ____ who lies, gambles, and abandons his debts, readers cannot help hoping that he will escape justice.
gre.clue: who lies, gambles, and abandons his debts

en: Cloudy or muddy (of liquid); confused
hook: TURBID: TURBulent water, all stirred up.
story: Turbid. After three days of heavy rain, the clear stream behind Joya's school turned thick and brown. Mud, leaves, and silt churned in the water, and nobody could see the fish anymore. The water was turbid: cloudy or muddy. Turbid can also describe confused thought or feeling, as in a turbid argument. It comes from the Latin turba, turmoil, as in turbulent. Do not confuse it with turgid, which means swollen or pompous. Synonyms: murky, muddy, cloudy.

gre.s: Once so clear that visitors could see pebbles three meters down, the lake has become ____ since mining began upstream, its waters now thick with silt.
gre.clue: its waters now thick with silt

en: Swollen; pompous and overly complex in style
hook: TURGID: TURNED rigid from swelling, swollen with big words.
story: Turgid. Ishita's classmate submitted an essay that began, "In the multifarious and labyrinthine matrix of contemporaneous paradigms, one must necessarily interrogate," and continued that way for twenty pages. The teacher wrote one word at the top: turgid, meaning pompous and overly complex in style. Literally, turgid means swollen, like a river in flood or a sprained ankle; turgid prose is swollen with big words. Do not confuse it with turbid, meaning muddy. Synonyms: bombastic, pompous, grandiloquent.

gre.s: The senator's speech was so ____, so swollen with grand abstractions and needless jargon, that the simple point she wished to make was entirely lost.
gre.clue: swollen with grand abstractions and needless jargon

en: Showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty
hook: VACUOUS: like a VACUUM, empty inside.
story: Vacuous. A television host asked a celebrity what she thought about climate change. She smiled and said, "I think the climate is really important, and change is good, so it is all very positive." Viewers laughed. Her answer was vacuous: showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty. It comes from the same root as vacuum and vacant: nothing inside. A vacuous stare is a blank, empty one. Synonyms: inane, vapid, mindless.

gre.s: The candidate's speeches, full of rousing slogans but devoid of any concrete policy proposals, struck most serious analysts as ____.
gre.clue: devoid of any concrete policy proposals
